Photograph: Danny Lawson/PA Prisons and probation Burnham urged to intervene over ‘zero-hours’ custody officers in private prison Exclusive: Prison officers’ union strongly opposes HMP Millsike offering flexible work escorting prisoners amid staff shortages Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Tue 18 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham is under pressure to intervene in a privately run prison that is seeking to recruit custody officers on zero-hours contracts for the first time across England and Wales’ prison estate. Managers at HMP Millsike, a category C prison for 1,500 prisoners near York operated by the outsourcing company Mitie, have signed off online adverts for £25-an-hour prisoner escort roles “on a flexible, task-based basis”. Mitie has submitted a proposal to the Prison Service to employ people on a zero-hours contract which is “under consideration”, a government official confirmed on Monday night . The £400m prison has about 350 empty cells because of a shortfall of staff, prison sources have confirmed. The POA, the prison officers’ union, has called on the prime minister to intervene in keeping with the government’s pledge to curb zero-hours contracts that undermine workers’ rights, security and stability. Burnham has faced mounting pressure over the government’s early prisoner release scheme aimed at freeing up capacity, after it was revealed that the killers of the police officer Andy Harper would be freed. While the prime minister has pledged that Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers will remain in prison, he has been told he cannot exempt specific offenders from early release without also keeping about 500 other offenders who have also been convicted of manslaughter locked up. The deputy general secretary of the POA, Mick Pimblett, said: “At a time when the government is releasing prisoners because of a chronic lack of cell space, Mitie is unable to fulfil its contractual obligations because they cannot recruit enough officers to safely staff the jail. Now they are trying to introduce zero-hours contracts by another name. Life behind bars in Britain’s surviving Victorian prisons – photo essay Read more “The POA rejects this attempt to bring casualised labour into the prison system. Prison officers are committed professionals working in a highly pressured, often hostile environment. Treating them in the same way as zero-hours contractors is disgraceful.” HMP Millsike, a training prison with up-to-date facilities, started taking prisoners in March 2025. A recent report expressed “serious concerns” over the jail, where violence levels were so high that members of the watchdog the Independent Monitoring Boards (IMB) said they only felt safe if they walked around in pairs. Adverts placed by the Sangfroid Group on behalf of Mitie say the new prison custody officers at Millsike will escort prisoners between prisons, courts and medical appointments – tasks currently performed by full-time prison officers. The advert reads: “Prison Custody Officer – Escort Duties, £25 per hour. Are you a former member of the UK Armed Forces, Blue Light Services, or Prison Service looking for flexible, meaningful work that fits around your existing commitments?” It continues: “Sangfroid Group is proud to be partnering with Mitie Care & Custody, the operator of HMP Millsike, to deliver an innovative and pioneering operational support model within the UK prison estate.” The role is to support “prisoner escort duties in locations near to the prison” and successful applicants will be given seven weeks of training, the advert says. “If you’re looking for more routine, predictable hours, we can offer regular rotational work. This would typically involve working up to 2-3 weeks each month on a rotation basis, with deployments of up to five consecutive days at a time. Alternatively, if you prefer greater flexibility, you can join our contingent workforce, supporting ad hoc operational requirements.” State-run prisons already recruit operation support-grade officers who staff gates and let visitors into reception. However, they are not supposed to escort, guard, handcuff or interact with prisoners, unlike Millsike’s new prison custody officers referred to in the advert. Mitie, which is paid about £33m a year to run the prison, has faced intense criticism over its management since it opened 17 months ago. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion In January, IMB said that during staff visits they noticed “inconsistent gate security”, with “doors and gates being left open”. A month later, Mitie replaced the director, who moved to a strategic role. There were more than 1,600 vacancies for prison officers in England and Wales in June, compared with 22,000 or so currently working, according to data. While 248 prison officers joined that month, another 256 left. According to Acas, the definition of a zero-hours contract is one where the employer does not give minimum working hours and the employee does not have to take any work offered. Mitie said it did not offer “zero-hours” contracts to Millsike employees, pointing out that Sangfroid Group provided “contingent workers” and was responsible for the terms and conditions of staff recruited through the advert. A Mitie spokesperson said: “HMP Millsike continues to operate in line with the ramp-up plans agreed with the Ministry of Justice, with staffing and recruitment aligned to the prison’s phased population buildup. We remain focused on maintaining a safe, secure and supportive environment for prisoners and colleagues.” A government spokesperson said: “Our dedicated prison officers work around the clock to keep our prisons running and the public safe, and prison officer contracts will always be compliant with employment law. “We inherited a prison capacity crisis after places increased by just 500 in 14 years, and are pulling every lever possible to fix this – building 14,000 new places with 3,200 already delivered.” Sangfroid Group has been approached for comment . Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania's National Liberal Party (PNL) and Save Romania Union (USR) have referred the recently adopted Integrity Law to the Constitutional Court (CCR), arguing that one of its key provisions violates the constitutional principle prohibiting the retroactive application of legislation, Ziarul Financiar reported. The law is a milestone under Romania's National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). If it is not enacted by August 31, Romania risks losing a EUR 771 million grant under the European Union's Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). The constitutional challenge focuses on an amendment adopted by Parliament at the initiative of the Social Democratic Party (PSD), which provides that local elected officials previously found to have been in a conflict of interest would lose their mandates once the new law enters into force, even though the legislation in force at the time did not impose such a sanction. PNL and USR argue that the provision breaches Article 15 of Romania's Constitution, which stipulates that laws apply only to future situations, except where new criminal provisions are more favourable to the accused. The amendment has been widely linked to the case of Timișoara Mayor Dominic Fritz. Romania's National Integrity Agency (ANI), with the finding subsequently upheld by the courts, determined that Fritz had been in a conflict of interest after approving an urban planning document involving a local councillor who had previously lent him money during an electoral campaign. Following the constitutional challenge, PSD accused PNL and USR on August 6 of jeopardising the EUR 771 million RRF grant by delaying the law's entry into force. The Social Democrats argued that referring the legislation to the Constitutional Court risks preventing Romania from meeting the August 31 deadline attached to the reform milestone. However, the party did not address the opposition's argument that the contested amendment may be unconstitutional because it applies sanctions retroactively. The Constitutional Court will now determine whether the disputed provisions comply with the Constitution. Its ruling will also determine whether the legislation can be promulgated in time for Romania to fulfil the relevant RRF commitment. Photograph: Christopher Oquendo/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Georgia Six Flags to reopen Goliath rollercoaster – but now with seatbelts after recent rider death Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem fell from ride earlier this month, spurring amusement park to temporarily shut it down Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.44 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 15.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Six Flags will install seatbelts on its Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia , after a rider plummeted to his death earlier this month. Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old father and educator, was thrown from his seat on the Goliath, a coaster that plunges riders down 165ft, before a second drop of 180ft. On his way down, he collided with the ride’s other cars. Georgia authorities have launched a probe into Kariem’s death. The gruesome fall prompted the park to temporarily close the Goliath and eight rides at five other parks. Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable Read more “What happened has deeply affected all of us at Six Flags. Safety has always been fundamental to the experience we provide for our guests,” the theme park’s CEO, John Reilly, wrote on Friday. Seatbelts will also be added to coasters with a similar restraint, he announced, although an exact list remains unclear. The Goliath features a lap bar that locks over a rider’s waist, a design from Bolliger & Mabillard. The park has also commissioned an independent review of the safety procedures for all of its attractions. “I know trust is earned through actions and not words,” Reilly said. “We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you.” The Six Flags Over Georgia fatal incident comes as the theme park is being sued over alleged bodily harm from its X2 ride at Magic Mountain. A recent CNN investigation uncovered a long history of brain injuries and at least two deaths linked to the ride. A group of past riders who say they sustained brain injuries on X2 has accused the park of having a defective coaster and negligence for allowing its continued operation, according to court documents. Six Flags permanently shut down the embattled X2 coaster in September.
